answer:
Using the Antoine equation, water's vapour pressure at 180 °C is about **10.0 bar (about 997 kPa)**.

I evaluated two constant sets that are valid at 180 °C:

| Antoine constants | Valid range | P at 180 °C | vs. IAPWS-95 (1002.8 kPa) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A = 8.14019, B = 1810.94, C = 244.485 (log10 P in mmHg, T in °C) | 99–374 °C | 997.4 kPa (9.97 bar) | −0.5 % |
| NIST: A = 3.55959, B = 643.748, C = −198.043 (log10 P in bar, T in K) | 379–573 K | 10.87 bar (1087 kPa) | +8.4 % |

- **Use the first set.** It is the one to quote and is within 0.5 % of the reference value.
- **The NIST set** is inside its stated range but still comes out 8 % high at 180 °C.
- **The usual textbook set** (A = 8.07131, B = 1730.63, C = 233.426) only holds from 1 to 100 °C, so it shouldn't be used here. Pushed to 180 °C anyway, it gives 1023.6 kPa.
- **Reference value:** 1002.8 kPa, which I computed with CoolProp (IAPWS-95, saturation pressure at 453.15 K).

All the figures above come from running each equation; none were recalled. No files were created.
